questions.short_title: Prehospital TXA lowers mortality in bleeding trauma
questions.question: What does the pooled randomised evidence say about prehospital TXA and 28-30 day mortality in trauma?
options: A rise in thromboembolic events
No clear reduction in mortality
Benefit only in isolated head injury
A reduction in mortality
questions.explanation: The three-trial pool showed lower 28-30 day mortality (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.68-0.95). The pool is small, and the TBI and in-hospital findings come from single trials.

questions.short_title: Bystander-attached AEDs linked with best OHCA survival
questions.question: In this registry cohort, 30-day survival after OHCA was highest when the first AED was attached by which responder group?
options: On-duty first responders
Community first responders
Bystanders
EMS
questions.explanation: Bystander attachment came with the highest 30-day survival (28%, vs 9.0% when EMS attached first), likely because it reflects earlier recognition and defibrillation. It's observational, so the responder type alone can't be credited with the difference.

questions.short_title: First responder alerts linked to more defibrillation
questions.question: How did community first responder activation affect bystander defibrillation as the distance to the nearest AED increased?
options: The benefit of activation grew as AED distance increased
Activation made no difference regardless of AED distance
Activation only helped when an AED was within 389 m
The benefit of activation shrank as AED distance increased
questions.explanation: Activation attenuated the drop in bystander defibrillation with increasing AED distance, with the predicted gap widest at 1,183 m (13.0% vs 4.8%). Because activation was not randomised and the survival gain was small with a lower confidence bound near zero, this is hypothesis-generating rather than practice-changing.

questions.short_title: Mobile app lifts simulated trauma performance
questions.question: What did paramedics using the mobile decision-support app achieve in the simulated trauma scenarios, compared with standard practice?
options: Better pain scores recorded during trauma management
Faster patient handover times at the receiving facility
Reduced scene times by several minutes on average
Completion of all critical actions far more often (35.4% vs 6.3%)
questions.explanation: Scenarios with the app met all critical actions 35.4% of the time versus 6.3% without, a large odds increase. This was simulated care at a single US agency, so it is hypothesis-generating and doesn't yet show a patient outcome benefit.

questions.short_title: Prehospital STEMI thrombolysis is value for money
questions.question: An Australian microsimulation modelled paramedic-administered prehospital thrombolysis for STEMI. What did it conclude about value for money?
options: Only cost-effective if thrombolysis is given within 10 minutes of ECG diagnosis
Not cost-effective compared with hospital-based thrombolysis
Cost-effective at AUD 16,750 per QALY gained, with results robust in sensitivity analysis
Cost-effective only from a societal perspective, not a health provider perspective
questions.explanation: The model estimated AUD 16,750 per QALY gained and the result held up across sensitivity analysis. It was a model against a hypothetical counterfactual rather than a randomised comparison, so long-term inputs came from published literature.

questions.short_title: Video calls showed no clear resource savings
questions.question: What did the CAM-VISION analysis find about video-assisted calls and prehospital resource use?
options: No difference in any measured outcome
A significant saving in cumulative unit time
Lower point estimates, but no significant difference
A significant drop in initial dispatch rates
questions.explanation: Dispatch, units and unit time all trended lower with video, but none reached statistical significance. It was a post hoc analysis not powered for resource outcomes, so the results are hypothesis-generating.

questions.short_title: Rescue breaths linked to better paediatric arrest survival
questions.question: In the Japanese paediatric OHCA registry, how did 30-day neurologically favourable survival compare between CPR types?
options: Compression-only CPR beat rescue-breathing CPR
Rescue-breathing CPR was highest, and no CPR was lowest
Any bystander CPR gave worse outcomes than no CPR
All three CPR types gave similar survival
questions.explanation: Survival was 16.0% with rescue-breathing CPR, 9.5% with compression-only and 3.6% with no bystander CPR. It's registry data, so children who got rescue breaths may have differed from those who didn't.

questions.short_title: Airway assistant training halved sim intubation time
questions.question: In this Australian simulation study, what difference did one hour of airway assistant training make when paramedics assisted an ICP intubating a continuously regurgitating manikin?
options: Training made no difference to intubation time or tube placement
Trained assistants were faster only when they had prior airway experience
Median intubation time roughly halved, with no oesophageal intubations in either group
Median intubation time roughly halved, but oesophageal intubations were more common in the trained group
questions.explanation: Trained pairs intubated in a median of 53 seconds versus 102.5 seconds, and neither group had oesophageal intubations. It was a pilot with only 12 participants in a simulated setting, so no patient outcomes yet.
